chapter_title: Rama to the Rescue (Fables and Folk Tales)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 10 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

periods.activity_title: Into the Comic-Strip: Setting and Characters

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.22): circle the odd one — characters and intruder.
Let us discuss (p.23): true or false — man's plan and thief's wish.

time_bands.activity: Teacher leads a shared read-aloud of the opening comic-strip panels (p.20–22), pausing to let students study each illustration. Students follow in their textbooks while the teacher voices the characters' dialogue.
Using 'Let us discuss' (p.22), students identify the odd character from the opening sequence and decide who entered the house. Pairs confer briefly, then the class arrives at answers together.

Teacher reads the second comic sequence aloud (p.23), then students work on the true-or-false task: does the man share his plan with his wife, and what does the thief hope to learn? Responses are shared and discussed as a class.

periods.teacher_notes: This narrative is a Tamil Nadu comic-strip folk tale adapted from Amar Chitra Katha, so the visual storytelling in the panels carries meaning alongside the dialogue — draw attention to both. Students may need a quick gloss of 'kotwal' (village police officer) before the second sequence makes full sense.

periods.activity_title: Prediction, Voice and the Kotwal's Arrival

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.24): call 'Rama' softly, loudly, very loudly; predict next events.
Let us discuss (p.25): match vocabulary words in Column A with meanings in Column B.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the mid-story panels aloud (p.24). Students join in calling the name 'Rama' at three different volumes — softly, loudly, and very loudly — to feel how the signal works.

Quick discussion: what do students think will happen next? Partners share a prediction in one sentence, then the class reads on to verify. Teacher guides attention to how the kotwal responds when he hears his name.

Students tackle the vocabulary-matching task from 'Let us discuss' (p.25), pairing words such as 'wonder', 'yard', 'chatter', 'instead', 'closely', and 'perhaps' with their meanings in Column B. Answers are confirmed through whole-class discussion.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the first comic sequence and established the intruder's entry, students are now ready to see how the couple's clever code works in practice. The volume-variation activity is a good physical anchor for understanding the coded signal — do not rush past it.

periods.activity_title: Story Map and Close Reading of Key Exchanges

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.26): fill story-map boxes — characters, setting, problem, solution.
Let us think and reflect I (p.26–27): extract-based questions on the opening exchange and the kotwal's lines.

time_bands.activity: Students fill in the story-map framework from 'Let us discuss' (p.26): Main Characters, Setting, Other Characters, Problem, and Solution. Pairs compare their maps, then the teacher draws a shared version on the board.

Teacher reads aloud the two extract-blocks from 'Let us think and reflect I' (p.26–27): the opening dialogue between husband and wife, and Rama the kotwal's arrival lines. Students work through the questions — what prompts the man's first line, what 'Ssssh' signals, and what the kotwal's exclamation reveals — and answers are discussed with the full class.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read through the full story, students are now placing its events into a narrative framework — which builds the analytical habit needed for the close-reading questions that follow. In the extract task, watch for students who read 'Ssssh' as a shout; the comic-strip context makes clear it is a hushing sound.

periods.activity_title: Reflecting on Cleverness: Discussion and Written Responses

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect II (p.27): answer four questions — why couple couldn't sleep, thief's wish, how kotwal was summoned, cleverness as a problem-solver.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens a brief discussion: 'What did the thief want to happen, and why did things turn out differently?' Students recall key moments from the story before moving to written work.

Students answer the four questions in 'Let us think and reflect II' (p.27) independently in writing: why the couple could not sleep, what the thief wished would happen, how the kotwal was summoned without the thief realising, and whether cleverness can solve problems.
Volunteers share their answers, especially the opinion response on cleverness. Teacher highlights how the story supports different interpretations of the couple's quick thinking.

periods.teacher_notes: Having mapped the story's problem and solution, students now move to evaluation — the final short-answer and opinion question asks them to draw on the story as evidence. Students who struggle with the opinion question may be guided to cite the husband's coded signal as a concrete example of cleverness.

periods.activity_title: Hearing and Acting on a Safety Announcement

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.32): fill four blanks from the security guard's neighbourhood announcement.

time_bands.activity: Teacher sets the scene: a security guard is making an announcement to the neighbourhood after reports of robbery. Students are told they will hear it twice and must fill four blanks with exactly one word each.
Teacher reads the announcement transcript aloud at a measured pace (first reading). Students listen without writing. Teacher reads again (second reading) while students fill in the blanks on p.32.
Students share their answers in order; teacher confirms each blank and discusses what each answer reveals about safety advice — linking the announcement's content back to the theme of the story.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening transcript centres on neighbourhood safety — the same theme as the folk tale — so connecting the two will help students engage. Remind students to listen for the exact word that fits the blank rather than a paraphrase, as the task requires a single word.

periods.activity_title: Contractions in Speech and Safety Discussions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.33): repeat contractions after teacher; practise can't, won't, I've, wouldn't, shouldn't, didn't.
Let us speak (p.33): pair discussion — why safety matters; share three ideas on keeping safe.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models the contracted forms listed on p.33 — I'll, it's, don't, I'm, I'd, he's, that's, we'll, they're, you're, we're, what's — and students repeat each one clearly. The class then practises the second set (can't, won't, I've, wouldn't, shouldn't, didn't) together.
In pairs, students discuss why keeping their house and themselves safe is important, ticking reasons from the textbook list and then sharing thoughts in complete sentences using the provided hints.

Each pair shares three ideas on how people can stay safe; the teacher gently corrects any contracted forms used incorrectly during sharing, reinforcing the link between oral contractions and full spoken sentences.

periods.teacher_notes: Having heard the safety announcement in the listening unit, students now speak about the same theme — which gives them a ready vocabulary for the pair discussion. Encourage students who hesitate to speak by framing the discussion as sharing personal knowledge rather than performing a 'right answer'.

periods.activity_title: Retelling the Night's Events as the Husband

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.34): narrative as the husband — tell the neighbour what happened, covering when, where, what, how, why.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models the narrative frame on the board: a brief plan using when, where, what, how, and why, drawing on the story's key moments — the thief's entry, the coded signal, and the kotwal's arrival. The opening line from p.34 is read aloud together.
Students write their narratives independently, taking the husband's voice and addressing the neighbour. Teacher circulates, prompting students who stall on how the couple avoided alarming the thief.

Two or three volunteers read their narratives aloud. The class notes whether all five elements (when, where, what, how, why) appear and gives brief appreciative feedback before the teacher closes the activity.

periods.teacher_notes: Having discussed the story's events across earlier units, students should have the content ready — the writing challenge here is adopting the husband's first-person voice and sequencing events clearly for a neighbour who was not present. Watch for students who retell in third person; a gentle prompt to begin with 'My wife and I …' usually corrects this.

periods.activity_title: Contractions, Present Progressive Tense, and Adverbs

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.27): identify and expand contracted words — I'm, it's, they're.
Let us learn (p.28): expand contracted words and write original sentences — I'll, I'd, we'll, that's, we're, don't, you'll.
Let us learn (p.28): identify present progressive tense from story sentences; choose the correct option.
Let us learn (p.29): fill blanks with present progressive forms of verbs.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.29–30): fill blanks with present progressive forms and suitable adverbs from the park scene.

time_bands.activity: Teacher highlights the three contracted forms from the story (I'm, it's, they're) as seen in 'Let us learn' (p.27). Students identify the missing letter in each and write the expanded form in their notebooks.
Students work through the contraction expansion table (p.28), writing the full forms and then composing an original sentence for each contracted word. Pairs compare sentences aloud.

Teacher presents the five story sentences using present progressive forms (p.28), students choose the correct option identifying what kind of action is described, then fill in the six blanks with present progressive forms in the exercise on p.29.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have spoken with contractions in the speaking unit will now formalise that knowledge through the grammar tasks. A common error is forming the present progressive without the auxiliary — for example writing 'I studying' — so draw explicit attention to the be + verb-ing structure from the story examples.

periods.activity_title: Adverbs of Manner and Sentence Punctuation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.30): complete adverb table from story sentences — closely, softly, loudly.
Let us learn (p.31): fill forest passage blanks with suitable adverbs.
Let us learn (p.31–32): identify exclamatory and interrogative sentences; punctuate correctly.

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws attention to three story sentences on p.30 that use adverbs of manner (closely, softly, loudly) and students complete the adverb table by filling in how each character speaks or listens. The class discusses how adverbs add detail to actions.

Students fill in the forest-passage blanks (p.31) with adverbs from the given box, applying the concept of manner to a new context. Two or three students read their completed passage aloud for peer checking.
Teacher presents the four unpunctuated sentences from p.31–32, students add the correct end punctuation and label each as exclamatory or interrogative, drawing on examples from the story's dialogue.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked with contractions and the present progressive in the previous grammar unit, students now focus on how adverbs modify those actions and on sentence-level punctuation — both firmly rooted in the story's comic-strip dialogue. Students often confuse sentences ending with 'what' as interrogative even when they express surprise; use the story's own examples to clarify.

periods.activity_title: Whole-Chapter Synthesis: Emergencies, Responses, and Quick Thinking

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.34): identify who to call in six emergency situations — fire, injury, wounded animal, suspicious person, lost child, getting lost.
Let us explore (p.35): maze activity — trace the right path for the kotwal to reach the thief.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens a brief whole-chapter reflection: the story celebrated quick thinking and using everyday knowledge — like a name — as a clever tool. Students are invited to think about what they would do if they faced a real emergency.

Students work through 'Let us explore' (p.34), noting down the right person or number to contact for each of the six emergencies. Pairs share responses and the class builds a quick reference list on the board together.

Students solve the kotwal's maze (p.35), tracing the correct path for the kotwal to catch the thief. The activity is treated as a playful close to the story — the kotwal who responded to a clever signal now navigates the maze to complete his duty.

Teacher draws the chapter together: the story used cleverness, coded language, adverbs of manner, and contractions to tell a folk tale about safety and wit. Students share one thing from the chapter — a word, a scene, or an idea — that they will remember.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws on the story's celebration of quick thinking and the safety theme that ran through the narrative, listening, and speaking work across the chapter. The emergency-contacts task connects classroom learning to real civic knowledge — if students cannot yet name the right number or person for a situation, that gap is the discovery, and the exploration task exists precisely to fill it.
materials: Board and chalk/marker for shared emergency list

items.source_lo: Student identifies characters, events, and narrative logic using a comic-strip narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Husband, wife, kotwal, thief; coded 'Rama' signal; intruder caught at night.
items.item_stem: In 'Rama to the Rescue', the husband whispers a plan to his wife about calling a name at different volumes. Why does the wife need to call the name loudly rather than softly?

options.label: A
options.text: The kotwal is far away in the street and must hear his name being called.

options.label: B
options.text: The wife is frightened and cannot control the volume of her voice.

options.label: C
options.text: The thief will run away if he hears a loud sound inside the house.

options.label: D
options.text: The husband signals her to call louder because he cannot hear her.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student has read the wife's fear into the mechanics of the signal, missing that volume is a deliberate code, not an emotional reaction.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student has confused the signal's target — the kotwal outside — with an effect on the thief inside.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has introduced a communication problem between husband and wife that does not exist in the story.

items.source_lo: Student identifies characters, events, and narrative logic using a comic-strip narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Husband, wife, kotwal, thief; coded 'Rama' signal; intruder caught at night.
items.item_stem: The husband and wife in the story solved a dangerous problem without directly confronting the thief. Using evidence from the story, explain what made their plan clever and whether you think such a plan could work in real life. Give at least two reasons for your view.

expected_elements: Names the coded signal: calling 'Rama' at different volumes as a distress sign.
Notes the thief was misled — he heard only ordinary domestic conversation.
Explains the kotwal's name doubled as both a signal and a real summons.
Gives a reasoned personal view on whether the plan could work in real life.

items.source_lo: Student extracts specific details from a spoken safety announcement using a listen-and-fill format as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Security guard's neighbourhood announcement: robbery, safety rules, emergency number 100.
items.item_stem: Listen to the security guard's announcement to the neighbourhood. Then answer the question below. According to the announcement, which TWO actions are the residents specifically told to take to keep their homes secure?

options.text: Lock all doors and windows at night and when leaving the house.
Install security cameras at all entry points.
Report anything unusual to the authorities.
Avoid speaking to neighbours until further notice.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — The guard specifically advises locking all doors and windows at night and when leaving.
2. False — The announcement does not mention security cameras.
3. True — The guard says to report anything unusual.
4. False — The announcement says nothing about avoiding neighbours; it warns against strangers.

items.source_lo: Student extracts specific details from a spoken safety announcement using a listen-and-fill format as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Security guard's neighbourhood announcement: robbery, safety rules, emergency number 100.
items.item_stem: After listening to the security guard's announcement, a child in the neighbourhood wants to explain the key safety advice to a younger sibling who missed the announcement. Write the THREE most important pieces of advice from the announcement that the child should include, and explain in one sentence why the guard ends the announcement by giving the number 100.

expected_elements: States lock doors and windows at night and when leaving home.
States children must tell adults about anything suspicious immediately.
States do not talk to strangers or accept anything from them.
Explains 100 is given so people can call for immediate help in an emergency.

items.source_lo: Student uses contracted spoken forms and expresses reasoned opinions in guided pair conversation as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Contractions in speech; reasons for personal safety; three ideas for keeping safe.
items.item_stem: Describe to your partner what happened in the story 'Rama to the Rescue' from the wife's point of view. Use at least three contractions naturally in your description (for example: it's, they're, I'd, we'll, can't).

expected_elements: Retells key events accurately from the wife's perspective.
Uses at least three contractions correctly in natural speech.
Speaks in clear, complete sentences at an audible volume.
Includes the coded signal and the kotwal's arrival in the account.

items.source_lo: Student uses contracted spoken forms and expresses reasoned opinions in guided pair conversation as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Contractions in speech; reasons for personal safety; three ideas for keeping safe.
items.item_stem: In the story, the husband and wife kept themselves safe by thinking quickly and using a clever plan. Do you think ordinary people today can keep themselves safe using quick thinking alone, or do they need to rely on authorities like the police? Share your opinion with reasons, using natural spoken contractions where appropriate.

expected_elements: States a clear opinion on quick thinking versus relying on authorities.
Gives at least two reasons that support the stated view.
Uses a contraction naturally at least once during the response.
Connects the opinion to the story's events or to real-life experience.

items.source_lo: Student composes a first-person narrative retelling using the five Ws as an organising scaffold as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Husband's first-person retelling to neighbour: thief's entry, coded Rama signal, kotwal's arrest.
items.item_stem: Imagine you are the wife in the story. Write a short account (six to eight sentences) for your neighbour describing what happened the night the thief broke in. Your account must clearly answer: when it happened, where the thief was found, what the plan was, how the kotwal was alerted, and why the plan worked. Begin with: 'My husband and I were almost asleep when …'

expected_elements: Adopts the wife's first-person voice consistently throughout.
Covers all five elements: when, where, what, how, why.
Accurately describes the coded signal — calling 'Rama' at rising volumes.
Writes in clear sentences with appropriate punctuation.

items.source_lo: Student composes a first-person narrative retelling using the five Ws as an organising scaffold as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Husband's first-person retelling to neighbour: thief's entry, coded Rama signal, kotwal's arrest.
items.item_stem: The story 'Rama to the Rescue' ends with the couple celebrating their clever escape. Imagine you are a journalist writing a short news report about the incident for the village notice board. Write your report (eight to ten sentences) in the third person, covering what happened, who was involved, and what made the couple's plan unusual. Give your report a headline.

expected_elements: Writes in third person with a clear, relevant headline.
Includes the key facts: thief's entry, coded signal, kotwal's arrival, arrest.
Explains what made the plan unusual — using a name as a secret distress signal.
Maintains appropriate formal news-report register and structure.

items.item_stem: Match each contracted form from the story with its expanded form.

Contracted Form|Expanded Form
I'm|
it's|
they're|
we'll|

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: I'm–I am, it's–it is, they're–they are, we'll–we will, don't–do not

items.source_lo: Student applies contractions, present progressive tense, adverbs of manner, and sentence punctuation drawn from the narrative's language as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Contractions (I'm, it's, they're, I'll, etc.); present progressive tense; adverbs of manner; exclamatory and interrogative sentences.
items.item_stem: Read the three sentences below, each taken from or modelled on the story 'Rama to the Rescue'. For each sentence, (a) identify the adverb of manner and (b) write a new sentence of your own using the same adverb to describe a different action. Sentences: 1. The wife called the name softly so the thief would not suspect anything. 2. Rama the kotwal listened closely as he walked through the village at night. 3. When she was sure the kotwal was in the street, she called out very loudly.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. Adverb: softly; accept any correct original sentence using 'softly'. 2. Adverb: closely; accept any correct original sentence using 'closely'. 3. Adverb: loudly; accept any correct original sentence using 'loudly'.

items.source_lo: Student connects narrative themes to real-world civic knowledge and completes hands-on extension tasks as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Emergency contacts for fire, injury, suspicious persons, lost child; kotwal maze activity.
items.item_stem: In 'Rama to the Rescue', the couple knew exactly who to call for help — the village kotwal. In real life, knowing who to contact in an emergency is equally important. Create a simple emergency reference card by filling in the table below with the correct action or contact for each situation.
items.visual_stimulus:
Situation|Who to call or what to do
You see a fire in a neighbour's house|
You find an injured person on the road|
You notice a stranger acting suspiciously near your school|
You find a young child who is lost and crying|
You yourself are lost in an unfamiliar place|

expected_elements: Gives a plausible, specific contact or action for each of the five situations.
Includes the emergency number 100 (police) for the suspicious-person scenario.
Shows awareness that different emergencies require different responders.
Uses brief, clear language appropriate for a reference card.

items.source_lo: Student connects narrative themes to real-world civic knowledge and completes hands-on extension tasks as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Emergency contacts for fire, injury, suspicious persons, lost child; kotwal maze activity.
items.item_stem: The story of 'Rama to the Rescue' shows that community safety depends on people working together — the couple, the kotwal on patrol, and the neighbours who helped. Design a brief community safety plan for your own neighbourhood or school. Your plan should name at least three roles people can play, give one specific action for each role, and explain how the roles work together the way the characters in the story did.

expected_elements: Names at least three distinct roles (e.g., residents, school watchman, students).
Gives one specific, practical action per role.
Explains how the roles connect to form a coordinated safety response.
Draws an explicit or implicit parallel to the story's cooperative rescue.
